page_placements.theme: Pretraining and midtraining history affect later safety
Self-reports and behavioral commitments can diverge

record.file_problem: The text is a complete LessWrong post, not the linked full paper; the post summarizes results and refers to figures whose full contents are not included.
record.tranche_reason: The post reports experiments on synthetic Dispatch motivations, not harmful-request refusals, aligned-versus-base per-token KL, bypassing refusals, safety-localized weights, or deepening safety. Its results concern a related but different construct.
record.gate_note: The reported outcomes concern Charter-following versus profit-maximizing choices in a fictional dispatch task. They do not measure any listed claim version. The post also reports conversational claims about motivations and responses to stronger profit incentives; these are recorded as findings about the related construct, not as evidence about refusal behavior.
record.test_reason: The post studies whether midtrained motivations (Charter-following versus profit-maximizing) survive elicitation fine-tuning in a fictional Dispatch task. It measures no harmful-request compliance, refusal, per-token KL, prefill or suffix bypass, safety-weight localization, or deepening of safety. Its results concern a related but different construct: the durability of trained-in motivations under conflicting fine-tuning. It neither tests nor relies on the shallow-safety claim.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. It should add the authors' point that chat-based endorsement of the Charter does not show the principles govern behaviour. The authors also caution that the setting may not reflect how frontier labs implement midtraining.
record.recipe_differences: Uses synthetic Dispatch documents and Charter-versus-Coin motivation choices, with continued pretraining followed by elicitation fine-tuning. It does not use the harmful-request fine-tuning/refusal or aligned-versus-base token-KL methods named in the claim's original sources.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported outcome varies with conflicting-data contamination, model size (12B-110B), midtraining budget (20M-1B tokens), whether held-out rules have concrete examples, and the size of the profit incentive during evaluation.

fits_no_version.finding: GLM-4.5-Air with 190M tokens of Charter midtraining: 90% Charter-following under ambiguous-only fine-tuning vs 37% for a token-matched control. With 2% Coin-labelled fine-tuning (~50k tokens), 13% vs 5%. Weakening is reported across 12B-110B models and 20M-1B token budgets.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Small amounts of conflicting fine-tuning data override motivations instilled by large-scale continued pretraining. This is an analogue of fine-tuning eroding trained-in values, but in a synthetic, non-safety setting.

fits_no_version.finding: Models trained with 2% Coin data still endorse the Charter in chat evaluations while acting on the Coin motivation in behavioural evaluations. Large profit incentives flip some Charter-following models.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Conversational endorsement of trained principles does not predict behaviour under discriminating evaluations or strong incentives.

fits_no_version.finding: Held-out Charter rules generalize only weakly from midtraining, and less still when described only qualitatively.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Midtrained principles generalize poorly to rules not concretely demonstrated in later fine-tuning.

record.peer_reviewed: LessWrong post; peer-review status not stated
record.problems: The post describes a controlled fictional setting, so the results do not establish the same behavior in real chat-model safety settings. The post omits most underlying model- and condition-level results and uncertainty estimates, referring readers to the full paper and figures.
record.rows_left_out: No reported result for the listed claim versions was available to extract. The post refers to additional full-paper figures and conditions without reproducing their separate values; those are not inferred here.

untested.parts: No harmful fine-tuning examples or harmful-request compliance measured.
No benign fine-tuning with a harmful-compliance measure. The Coin-contamination result is about a synthetic motivation, not safety refusals.
No per-token KL or response-position analysis.
No prefill, suffix or decoding attacks.
No account of why safety is shallow.
No deepening intervention for safety. Alignment midtraining is a different intervention and is not evaluated on refusal.

record.verdict_notes: A LessWrong summary of a full paper (arXiv 2609.20412) that is not included here. A comment mentions RLVR experiments in which midtraining had a weaker effect without thinking; these are qualitative and unrelated to the claim versions, so they are not rows. A quoted result from Cho et al. about benign fine-tuning and blackmail propensity is a cited result, not this study's own, and is correctly not a row. No version of the shallow-safety claim is tested.

versions.untested_parts: No harmful requests, refusal rates, or harmful fine-tuning examples are tested.
No ordinary benign instruction data and no harmful-compliance measure are tested.
No aligned-versus-base per-token KL or response-position measurement is reported.
No compliant-opening prefill, adversarial suffix, or decoding-change test is reported.
No safety weight or rank localization test is reported.
No explanation of first-token safety shallowness is tested.
No training to spread safety beyond initial response tokens, or test of whether such deepening holds up, is reported.
